narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor, as a score of 40 is notably higher than the average of 37 among accepted students. This gave a meaningful push toward the likelihood of passing the bar.

However, two other factors pulled more strongly in the opposite direction. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 was substantially below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this lower academic performance significantly increased the model's estimate of bar exam failure. Similarly, your third-year law school grades placed you in the third decile, well below the average of roughly sixth decile for accepted students. This recent academic standing also pushed the prediction noticeably toward failure.

Although your middle-income background and plan to attend full-time are fairly typical among applicants, they did not offset the academic signals. 

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score even further, or explore schools with different admission thresholds. You may also want to speak with an admissions counselor about how to best present your full profile in a future application. (218 words)
